title: About
text:
I’m Aaron Cochran, a Research Systems Specialist on an interagency research team in state government. Our work serves more than one agency.
In practice that means I’m part data scientist, part platform administrator. I’m responsible for infrastructure, governance and research tooling: the systems researchers use to do careful work with sensitive data.

title: About
text:
Between research and infrastructure
I don’t sit firmly in one camp. I’m not purely a researcher, and I’m not purely an infrastructure engineer. I work in the space between them, where research needs systems that can actually support it.
On the infrastructure side, I build out the platforms our team works on, train staff to use them, set the standards we follow, and manage our GitHub. On the research side, I work directly with researchers to productionize their code, so that analysis can become something other people can run, rely on and use.
That position is part of why our work has shifted from delivering reports and papers to building research tools that put the research to use. We still write reports, but we publish them as HTML on Posit Connect so they’re accessible to staff who use screen readers. We also build simulations that help leadership and management weigh decisions before they make them.

title: About
text:
What I work on

Research platforms. Standing up and governing Posit Team on Snowflake: environments, access, promotion workflows and documentation.
Standards and training. Developing the conventions our team works by and teaching staff how to use the tools.
Research tools and accessible publishing. Turning findings into things people can use: accessible HTML reports and simulations that support decisions.
Record linkage. Probabilistic matching and identity resolution across agencies, designed so data can be shared without over-sharing.
Models in production. Moving models out of notebooks and into versioned, documented APIs with vetiver and plumber.

I work in R (using Positron), with Python alongside, across Snowflake, SQL Server, GitHub, Databricks, AWS and Azure.

I run tabletop RPGs, self-host the server my group plays on, and write about it here now and then. I’m also an avid PC gamer, hiker, photographer, and worldbuilder, and a very lucky husband and dad.

title: Hello, world
text: Welcome to my personal website. I’m Aaron Cochran, a Research Systems Specialist on an interagency research team in state government. Our work serves more than one agency.

title: Hello, world
text:
From analyst to systems builder
I’ve spent more than ten years in state government, and my role has changed a lot in that time. I started as a research analyst, leading interagency research projects with partners from other state agencies.
Along the way, I fell in love with the technical side of the job and started spending my spare time at work building durable systems and workflows for my teammates. I brought GitHub into our process to make our research more reproducible and transparent. In 2017 I led the procurement of our first machine learning server, Microsoft Machine Learning Server, which ran Microsoft’s own distribution of R. That server became the backbone for the predictive models my team built for agency programs. Microsoft retired the product in 2022, and in 2023 I migrated our remaining production model to open-source R so it could keep running.

title: Hello, world
text:
What I work on now
Today I lead our team’s research infrastructure. I led the procurement of our Posit Team environment, which runs in Snowpark Container Services as a Snowflake Native App, and I’m its administrator. That modern, scalable platform now hosts the production models and APIs our team builds, including some of the work I’m proudest of. I hope to write about it here in more detail.

title: Hello, world
text:
Off the clock
Outside of work, I’m the lucky father of two young kids. When they aren’t keeping me busy with art projects, outdoor play, Fortnite matches and Minecraft builds, I love reading, creative writing and running tabletop RPGs. For more than a decade, I’ve had the good fortune of leading the same core group of friends through weekly adventures.

Technical: the platforms, pipelines and tools behind our work.

I’ll do my best to keep posts short, interesting and relevant. I’m glad you’re here, and I hope you find something worthwhile.

title: What Are You Going to Do With It?
text:
The scenarios in this post are hypothetical, written to illustrate a pattern rather than describe any particular program or request.
Imagine a program asks whether the lunar cycle explains their call volume. Not just that some weeks bring more calls, but that those weeks bring more complicated calls too.
It’s a charming question, and it’s easy to see where it comes from. Staff who spend their days on the phones notice patterns, and a full moon is a tidy story for a chaotic week.
It’s also a good example of what I think of as a “nice to know” question: one where the answer might be interesting, but nobody can say what would change if we had it.
I’m part of an interagency research team in state government. We don’t run a data request desk, and the difference matters, because questions like this one are expensive.

title: What Are You Going to Do With It?
text:
Nothing about it is quick
From the outside, answering a question looks like a lookup. Someone has the numbers somewhere, so you pull them.
In practice, the data a program needs usually lives in more than one system, built at different times by different teams for different purposes. They don’t share an identifier. They define the same word differently. One counts a person once, another counts every contact. One records when something happened, another records when it was entered.
Linking them in a way that holds up for research means a long series of decisions:

How do I decide two records are the same person?
What do I do when I’m not sure?
Which definition of “active” are we using, and who agreed to it?
What are we allowed to combine, and under what protections?

None of those decisions is visible in the final number. All of them can change it. That’s the hidden work, and it costs the same whether the question matters or not.

title: What Are You Going to Do With It?
section: The expensive question is the one with no decision attached
text:
The expensive question is the one with no decision attached
Back to the moon. Suppose I spent weeks linking call logs to case records to measure “complexity,” then found a lunar effect, or didn’t. What would the program do differently on Monday?
The better question sits right underneath: what drives the busy, complicated weeks, and can we plan for them? That one has real answers. Maybe complex calls follow benefit notices, deadlines, or system changes. Those are things a program can staff, train, and communicate around.
Same data, same linking work, but one version changes what happens next and the other doesn’t.

title: What Are You Going to Do With It?
section: The slow slide toward smaller slices
text:
The slow slide toward smaller slices
The moon question is the dramatic case. The common one is quieter.
Picture an analysis that’s been delivered, and the response is, “Great, can we see it for just this region?” Then: “Just this region, for people under 25?” Then: “What about just the ones who also had this other thing?”
Each request sounds small. But each one tends to ask for something new:

Smaller groups are noisier. At some point you’re no longer describing a pattern, you’re describing a handful of people. The numbers jump around for reasons that have nothing to do with the program.
Smaller groups are riskier. The fewer people in a cell, the easier it is to work out who they are. That’s a privacy problem, and sometimes the right answer is that we can’t show it.
Every new cut can mean new linkage. Adding a characteristic often means pulling in another source and redoing the matching decisions.

“Slice it a different way” isn’t a bad request. The trouble is when it arrives without a reason. What would you learn from seeing it this way that you can’t see now? And what would you do about it?

title: What Are You Going to Do With It?
text:
The question worth asking
So I ask one, as gently as I can:

“What would you do differently if the answer came back high, versus low?”

This isn’t gatekeeping. Often there’s a real answer, and we get to a sharper question together. Sometimes the person was really asking something else, like the staffing question above. And sometimes the honest answer is “nothing, I was just curious,” which is fine to say out loud. It’s just not a good use of weeks of linkage work.
A question that’s ready for research usually has three things:

A decision or action it could inform.
A population big enough to say something stable about.
A comparison that means something: compared to what, or over what period?

title: What Are You Going to Do With It?
text:
Why this matters
Time spent chasing facts that lead nowhere is time not spent on the questions that could improve a program. A research team has limited capacity, and it’s worth protecting for the questions that matter.
Curiosity is where most good questions start. The work is helping it find its way to something a program can act on.

title: You Get the Data You Pay For
text:
Most of the research I do in human services runs on administrative data. That isn’t because it’s the best data for the job. It’s because it’s the data that exists.
Administrative data is a byproduct of running a program. Someone applies for benefits, a caseworker determines eligibility, a payment goes out, a case closes. Each step leaves a record, and those records pile up into a large, longitudinal, often linkable dataset that researchers like me are grateful to have. But none of it was collected to answer research questions. It was collected to run the program and to show the federal government that the program follows the rules.
That difference matters more than people expect.

title: You Get the Data You Pay For
section: What administrative data is built to answer
text:
What administrative data is built to answer
Benefit programs like SNAP and TANF, and services like child welfare, carry heavy federal reporting requirements. Those requirements largely decide what gets recorded, how it’s defined, and how carefully it’s checked. If a field feeds a federal report, it tends to be well defined and fairly complete. If it doesn’t, it may be optional, free text, inconsistently used, or missing entirely.
So administrative data is very good at questions like:

How many people were served, and for how long?
Were eligibility decisions made on time?
How much was paid out, and to whom?

It is much weaker at the questions programs care about most:

Are families more economically stable a year after they leave the program?
Did a new service improve child well-being, or only shift when cases close?
Which parts of the program make a difference, and for whom?

These outcome questions often depend on things the system never captures: someone’s wellbeing, the stability of their housing, their experience with the program, what happened after they left. You can’t analyze a variable that was never recorded.

title: You Get the Data You Pay For
section: What quasi-experimental methods can and can’t do
text:
What quasi-experimental methods can and can’t do
When a randomized trial isn’t possible, which in public programs is most of the time, we turn to quasi-experimental designs: difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, propensity score methods, interrupted time series, and similar tools. I use them often, and they are powerful. Applied carefully, they can get much closer to a causal estimate than a simple before-and-after comparison.
But they have limits that no amount of statistical skill removes:

They can only estimate effects on outcomes that were measured. If the outcome a program cares about isn’t in the data, no design recovers it.
They depend on assumptions the data can’t always test. Parallel trends, no unmeasured confounding, a clean cutoff. Administrative data rarely holds the variables we’d need to check those assumptions properly.
They inherit every quality problem in the source data. A sophisticated model built on inconsistent records gives a precise-looking answer to a fuzzy question.

Quasi-experimental methods help us get the most out of the data we have. They don’t replace data that was collected on purpose to answer a specific question.

title: You Get the Data You Pay For
section: Purposeful data collection has real costs
text:
Purposeful data collection has real costs
When a program wants to know whether it’s working, the natural next step is to collect new data: a survey, interviews, focus groups, a structured intake form. This is often the right move. What gets underestimated, almost everywhere in government, is what doing it well costs.
Good data collection needs:

Planning. Defining the question, deciding what to measure, choosing a sample, and working out how the data will be analyzed before anything is collected. This is the step that most often gets skipped, and skipping it is the main reason surveys end up measuring satisfaction when the real question was impact.
Instrument design. Writing survey questions that are clear, unbiased, and actually measure the concept you care about takes training and testing. A question that seems obvious to the person writing it can mean three different things to respondents.
Privacy and ethics review. Human services data is sensitive. Consent, data sharing agreements, and protections for participants all take time and expertise.
Staffing. Someone has to recruit participants, follow up on non-response, manage the data, and analyze it. Qualitative work needs even more: facilitators, note-takers, transcription, and careful coding by people trained to do it.
Infrastructure. Data needs to be captured in systems that validate entries, restrict access, track changes, and connect to the rest of the analytic environment.

None of this is exotic. It’s standard research practice. It just isn’t free, and it rarely appears in a program’s budget.

title: You Get the Data You Pay For
text:
The spreadsheet problem
When the infrastructure isn’t there, people make do. Across government, a lot of program-level data collection happens in Excel. That isn’t carelessness. It’s what’s available, it’s familiar, and it gets the job done in the moment.
But spreadsheets weren’t designed for data collection. There’s no validation on entry, so a date ends up typed three different ways. There’s no controlled vocabulary, so one category shows up under five spellings. Files get copied, renamed, and emailed around, so no one is sure which version is current. Columns change meaning partway through a year. By the time the data reaches an analyst, a large share of the effort goes into cleaning it, and some errors can’t be fixed because the information needed to fix them was never captured.
These are system problems, not people problems. Give the same staff a well-designed form with validation and a shared database, and data quality improves right away.

title: You Get the Data You Pay For
text:
Why this keeps happening
It’s easy to read all of this as a criticism of the people doing the work. It isn’t. The program staff I work with care a great deal about the families they serve and want to know whether what they’re doing helps. The constraints are structural:

Funding follows compliance. Federal requirements come with deadlines and consequences. Evaluation usually doesn’t, so it’s often the first thing cut when budgets tighten.
Data collection is treated as overhead. It’s rarely budgeted as part of running a program, so it competes with direct services, and direct services almost always win.
Staff capacity is stretched thin. Teams running programs are often already at or past capacity. Designing and running a rigorous data collection effort on top of that isn’t realistic without dedicated support.
Research methods training isn’t part of most program roles. That’s reasonable. We don’t expect researchers to be eligibility experts either. But it means survey design and measurement often fall to people who were never given the tools for it.

The result is a system very good at counting what it does and much less able to learn whether it’s working.

title: You Get the Data You Pay For
text:
What would help
I don’t think the answer is a large new research operation in every program. Some smaller shifts would go a long way:

Start with the question. Before collecting anything, write down what decision the data will inform and what you’d need to know to make it.
Bring research staff in early. An hour of consultation during design saves weeks of cleaning and reanalysis later, and can mean the difference between data that answers the question and data that can’t.
Budget for data collection as part of the program. If an outcome matters enough to ask about, it matters enough to fund measuring it properly, including staff time and infrastructure.
Collect less, but on purpose. A short, well-designed instrument that measures the right outcome beats a long survey that measures everything loosely.
Invest in shared infrastructure. Validated forms, secure databases, and standard definitions benefit every program that uses them and make each new collection cheaper than the last.

Administrative data will always be the backbone of public-sector research, and it should be. It’s comprehensive, longitudinal, and already paid for. But if we want to know whether programs are actually improving people’s lives, we have to be willing to collect the data that question requires, and be honest about what that takes.
